text: Lesson 29 designed Harlow Creek Logistics' landing zone and network. This lesson writes that design down as real ADRs, in the context, options, decision, and consequences format, then builds a disaster recovery plan with concrete RTO and RPO targets on top of the same design.

ADR-001 documents the hub-and-spoke decision itself, including its honest cost: shared services get deployed and patched once instead of six times, but the hub becomes a dependency every spoke relies on for egress and name resolution. That consequence gets written down on purpose, not hidden, because it becomes directly relevant two decisions later.

ADR-003 is the decision that matters most: the hub's shared services -- its firewall, gateway, and DNS resolver -- get their own explicit RTO and RPO, deployed to both the primary and secondary region, at least as strict as the tightest spoke that depends on them. This ADR exists specifically to close a gap that a review board can otherwise miss entirely.

RTO and RPO get set per tier based on actual business impact, not as one number for the whole organization. Customer Portal gets the tightest target because it's public-facing; Fleet Analytics gets the loosest because stale internal reporting is tolerable for a day; and the shared hub services are set to match the tightest tier that depends on them, not an average across all three.

A disaster recovery plan that's never tested is a guess, so Harlow Creek schedules a quarterly game day with three required checks in order: fail over Customer Portal and confirm its RTO is actually met, fail over the hub itself and confirm spokes can still reach the internet and resolve DNS, then fail back and confirm no drift was introduced. The second step is the one most DR plans skip.

Lesson 30 turned Lesson 29's design decisions into three documented ADRs and a tiered DR plan with a real, three-step test. Lesson 31 is a case study of a different, fictional organization that built a similar-looking design without writing anything like ADR-003 -- and shows exactly what that gap costs when a real outage hits.
